title:
The Heater Is Not the Thermal System
Dr. Moh Kolbehdari
gist: A dense technical essay arguing that thermo-optic phase stability in silicon photonics stops being a device problem once the die is packaged: the heater sets local temperature, but the package thermal field — neighboring electronics, interposer, TIM, lid, cooling — determines the refractive-index distribution and therefore the actual optical phase. The practical conclusions are that better cooling does not automatically mean better phase control, that open-loop calibration cannot survive workload and package variation, and that packaging must enter the photonic design flow far earlier, with closed-loop control and telemetry.

themes.theme: Package, not heater, sets optical phase

insights.claim: In a packaged silicon-photonics system the heater only establishes the intended thermal input, while the package determines the thermal field and the thermal field determines whether the intended optical phase remains stable.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Reassigns the yield and margin risk in photonic products from the device designer to the OSAT/packaging layer — a cost and schedule item most photonics roadmaps under-model.
insights.quote: And the thermal field determines whether the intended optical phase remains stable.
insights.locator: But that description becomes incomplete

insights.claim: The canonical thermo-optic chain of electrical current to Joule heating to temperature rise to refractive-index change to optical phase shift is incomplete for packaged devices; the real chain inserts a package thermal field between local heating and the index distribution.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: The corrected causal chain is the model any photonic-packaging simulation flow must implement — a checkable capability when assessing EDA/multiphysics vendors.
insights.quote: Electrical current → Joule heating → temperature rise → refractive-index change → optical phase shift
insights.locator: The chain is straightforward

insights.claim: The phase shifter remains the actuator but the package becomes part of the plant being controlled, converting a photonic device problem into a control-systems problem.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Control-theoretic framing means the required skill set — and vendor stack — for photonics shifts toward sensing and closed-loop control, not just optics.
insights.quote: The phase shifter remains the actuator, but the package becomes part of the plant being controlled.
insights.locator: The relevant chain becomes

insights.claim: A photonic die is heated by many sources beyond its own heaters — neighboring thermo-optic elements, modulators and optical amplifiers, electronic drivers, DSPs, lasers and laser-coupling regions, voltage regulators and power-delivery structures, adjacent compute or I/O chiplets, and changing system workloads.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Enumerates why co-packaged optics is harder than the roadmaps imply: every added chiplet is another uncontrolled heat source into the optical plane.
insights.locator: The package reshapes the temperature field

insights.claim: Heat also leaves through many paths — silicon substrate, oxide and dielectric layers, underfill or bonding materials, interposers and package substrates, thermal interface materials, heat spreaders, lids and cold plates, and surrounding air or coolant — so the temperature around one phase shifter depends on far more than its own heater current.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Each of these is a separately sourced material with its own tolerance — the supply-chain surface area for photonic phase drift is wide.
insights.quote: The temperature surrounding one phase shifter therefore depends on much more than its own heater current.
insights.locator: Heat also leaves through several paths

insights.claim: Device-level thermal crosstalk is interaction between nearby structures, whereas package-level thermal coupling is interaction through the shared thermal environment — a distinction that means spacing and isolation trenches cannot solve the second class.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Separates a solved problem from an unsolved one; teams reporting good device-level crosstalk numbers may still fail in-package.
insights.quote: Device-level thermal crosstalk is interaction between nearby structures. Package-level thermal coupling is interaction through the shared thermal environment.
insights.locator: This leads to an important distinction

insights.claim: System-level thermal crosstalk propagates over larger distances and through different paths than device crosstalk: a neighboring electronic die heats the shared interposer, a package lid spreads heat from one region toward another, and underfill, substrate and heat-spreader materials redirect heat in ways not visible from the isolated phase-shifter design.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Means phase-drift failures can be traced to material choices made by a packaging team with no visibility into optical specs — an organizational failure mode as much as a physical one.
insights.locator: But system-level crosstalk can occur over larger distances

insights.claim: Thermal crosstalk, static power and response time continue to limit dense integration of thermo-optic phase shifters despite their continued widespread use.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Names the three specific ceilings on photonic switch-fabric density — the metrics to watch for any claimed breakthrough in programmable photonics.
insights.quote: Thermo-optic phase shifters remain widely used, but thermal crosstalk, static power and response time continue to limit dense integration.
insights.locator: The traditional device trade-off

themes.theme: Better cooling is not better phase control

insights.claim: A more thermally conductive package removes unwanted heat but degrades thermo-optic tuning, because tuning deliberately relies on maintaining a local temperature difference — so the package must perform two conflicting tasks at once.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the default packaging instinct of maximizing conductivity; a design rule that changes material selection for co-packaged optics.
insights.quote: But thermo-optic tuning deliberately relies on a local temperature difference.
insights.locator: Better cooling does not automatically mean better phase control

insights.claim: The correct packaging target for photonics is not maximum thermal conductivity but a controlled thermal transfer function between electrical power, package temperature and optical phase.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Redefines the spec a photonic package is bought against — vendors selling only on W/mK are optimizing the wrong variable.
insights.quote: It is a controlled thermal transfer function between electrical power, package temperature and optical phase.
insights.locator: The correct target is not simply maximum

insights.claim: Specific packaging trade-offs each cut both ways: a highly conductive heat spreader reduces gradients but increases coupling between distant regions, a thermally isolating structure reduces tuning power but slows response, and a soft TIM accommodates mechanical variation but gives a different thermal path than a thin solder or adhesive TIM.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A concrete trade-off table for evaluating photonic package designs — no single material choice dominates, which is why the problem needs system-level optimization.
insights.locator: For example:

insights.claim: A package optimized for peak junction temperature may not minimize optical phase drift, and aggressive local cooling may increase the heater power needed for the same phase shift.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Peak-Tj-optimized packaging inherited from digital logic actively raises photonic tuning power — a hidden power-budget penalty in co-packaged optics.
insights.quote: a package optimized for peak junction temperature may not minimize optical phase drift;
insights.locator: For example:

insights.claim: The device-level thermo-optic trade-off is that better thermal isolation lowers power but slows cooling and raises the thermal time constant, while faster heat removal speeds switching but raises the power needed to hold a temperature.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: The efficiency-versus-speed frontier is fundamental, not an engineering gap — it caps how fast thermo-optic switching fabrics can ever be at a given power.
insights.quote: A well-isolated heated waveguide requires less electrical power because less heat escapes into the surrounding material. However, that same thermal isolation can slow cooling and increase the device’s thermal time constant.
insights.locator: The traditional device trade-off

insights.claim: The calibrated relationship between heater current or voltage and observed optical response does not stay constant — it shifts with ambient temperature, package warm-up, neighboring activity, material ageing, heater-resistance drift, TIM redistribution, cooling-system variation and accumulated thermal stress.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Factory calibration is not a durable asset for photonic products; field drift becomes a reliability and warranty exposure.
insights.quote: An open-loop value that produced the correct phase yesterday may produce a slightly different result under another operating condition.
insights.locator: Calibration cannot be separated from packaging

insights.claim: Calibration drift matters most in large photonic switching fabrics, wavelength-selective systems and programmable photonic circuits, where many tunable elements must remain aligned simultaneously.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: The scaling penalty falls hardest on exactly the high-value photonic products — optical switching for datacenters — which is why they keep slipping.
insights.locator: This becomes increasingly important in large photonic switching fabrics

insights.claim: Solving phase stability requires more than a better heater: optical monitors, local temperature sensors, background calibration, workload-aware control, closed-loop phase adjustment, thermal-state estimation and package-level telemetry.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Implies real silicon-area and BOM content for sensing and control in every photonic product — an addressable market adjacent to the optics themselves.
insights.quote: The optical system must know not only what command was sent to the heater, but whether the intended phase state was actually achieved and maintained.
insights.locator: The solution may require more than a better heater

themes.theme: Packaging must move left in the design flow

insights.claim: Introducing the package after photonic devices are designed and characterized is too late for thermo-optic systems; package-level phase stability should influence chiplet placement, heater-to-resonator distance, interposer and substrate material selection, underfill and bonding properties, TIM selection and bond-line control, heat-spreader geometry, sensor placement and control-loop architecture.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A shift-left mandate that creates demand for coupled electro-thermal-optical co-design tooling before tapeout — an EDA and simulation market signal.
insights.quote: The package is often introduced after the photonic devices have already been designed and characterized.
insights.locator: Packaging must enter the photonic design flow earlier

insights.claim: Manufacturing tolerances, die-attach conditions, TIM variation and material-property distributions can create different thermal behavior across otherwise identical packages, so nominal-geometry models are insufficient.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Unit-to-unit thermal variance implies per-unit calibration or closed-loop control at volume — a direct hit to photonic assembly cost and test time.
insights.quote: Manufacturing tolerances, die-attach conditions, TIM variation and material-property distributions may create different thermal behavior across otherwise identical packages.
insights.locator: The model should also include more than the nominal geometry

insights.claim: A complete realization flow must connect device design to package thermal model to manufactured structure to measured phase response to closed-loop control, rather than stopping at simulation.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Defines the full toolchain a photonics program must own; gaps in this chain are where programs stall between demo and production.
insights.quote: Device design→package thermal model→manufactured structure→measured phase response→closed-loop control
insights.locator: A complete realization flow should connect

themes.theme: Generalization to chiplets and heterogeneous integration

insights.claim: Integrating functional blocks does not guarantee the combined system behaves as intended — interfaces, materials, environment and control architecture determine whether device performance survives system realization.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: The general case against assuming chiplet composability; a reason integration timelines slip that has nothing to do with interconnect standards.
insights.quote: Integrating functional blocks does not guarantee that the combined system will behave as intended.
insights.locator: This is the same lesson appearing across heterogeneous integration

insights.claim: As electronics, photonics, memory, power delivery and cooling become more tightly integrated, the package is no longer a passive container but participates directly in system behavior — shaping temperature, stress, optical alignment, phase stability, electrical return paths, calibration requirements and reliability over time.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Elevates advanced packaging from cost center to performance determinant — supports a structurally higher value capture for packaging and materials suppliers.
insights.quote: the package is no longer a passive container. It participates directly in system behavior.
insights.locator: Beyond the phase shifter

insights.claim: A device can meet its specifications on a test structure and still fail to maintain the same operating margin inside a heterogeneous package, which is why future chiplet architectures must move beyond component integration toward coupled system realization.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Test-structure results are a weak signal for in-package performance — discount photonics and chiplet claims that rest on standalone device data.
insights.quote: A device may meet its specifications on a test structure and still fail to maintain the same operating margin inside a heterogeneous package.
insights.locator: Beyond the phase shifter

insights.claim: Thermo-optic tuning should be treated as an electrical, thermal, optical, packaging and control problem simultaneously, not as a photonic-device optimization problem.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Multi-domain framing tells you which vendors can actually serve this market: those with coupled multiphysics plus control competence, not point-tool optics players.
insights.quote: It is an electrical, thermal, optical, packaging and control problem.
insights.locator: Conclusion
